opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that first year was honestly one of the hardest periods of my life. I came to MIT for my PhD with a lot of excitement, but I quickly found myself in a place where I was working very hard on things that didn't feel like *mine*. I was trying to fit into what I thought a successful PhD student should be doing: chasing papers, following directions that looked promising on paper, measuring myself against people around me who all seemed incredibly brilliant. And at some point I realized I wasn't happy, and I wasn't even sure the work mattered to me.

There was a moment where I seriously thought, maybe this isn't for me, maybe I should just leave and do something else. What pulled me back wasn't some dramatic breakthrough. It was more that I sat down and asked myself a very simple question: if nobody was evaluating me, what would I actually want to build?

And the answer was pretty clear. Since I was young I loved writing code and making things move on the screen, physics simulation, graphics, things you can see and play with. And I had this persistent frustration that writing high-performance simulation code was way too painful. You spend weeks fighting with low-level optimization, data structures, GPU details, instead of thinking about the physics or the idea itself. That frustration eventually became the seed of Taichi, the programming language.

So what that near-dropout experience taught me is that the work I should pursue has to come from something I genuinely care about, a problem I personally feel, not just something that looks good on a CV. When you work on something like that, the motivation is internal. You don't need someone pushing you, and you're willing to go through the boring and difficult parts because you really want the thing to exist.

The second lesson was about impact. I started asking not just "can I publish this?" but "will people actually use this?" Building tools that let many other people do their work better felt far more meaningful to me than optimizing for one more incremental paper. That shift in mindset shaped the rest of my PhD and, honestly, everything I've done since, including starting a company around it.

So in a strange way, I'm grateful for that low point. If things had gone smoothly in the first year, I might have just kept going on autopilot, and never figured out what I really wanted to do.

r001.rationale: He says internal motivation makes him willing to work through difficult, boring parts when he cares about the work, but does not clearly state that this enables extraordinary effort.

r002.rationale: He says the experience taught him to pursue work he genuinely cares about rather than work chosen just because it looks good, after realizing he had been trying to fit expectations.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, that first year was rough. I had come from Tsinghua with a very clear picture of what I was supposed to be: the person who publishes a lot, who wins the awards, who gets the "right" kind of recognition. And when I got to MIT, I kept chasing that. I was taking on projects because they looked impressive on paper, not because I actually cared about them. And I burned out. There was a period where I genuinely thought about leaving. I wasn't sleeping well, I wasn't producing anything I was proud of, and I started wondering whether I even belonged in research.

What pulled me out of it was actually going back to the thing I had been doing since I was a kid, which was just writing code for fun. I started tinkering with physics simulation, not for a paper deadline, just because I found it beautiful. Watching snow or fluid come out of a few hundred lines of code felt almost magical to me. And I noticed something: I could work on that for fourteen hours and not feel tired. That was the opposite of how I felt about the "prestigious" projects.

So the lesson I took away was pretty simple, though it took me a while to internalize it. The work you should pursue is the work you'd do even if nobody was watching. For me, that meant building tools, making it easier for other people to write high-performance code. That eventually became Taichi, and later it became the reason I started a company. But none of that would have happened if I'd kept forcing myself down a path that looked good from the outside.

The other thing I learned is that almost quitting isn't a failure signal. It's a feedback signal. It's your mind telling you there's a mismatch between what you're doing and what you value. If I hadn't hit that wall, I think I would have spent years optimizing for the wrong thing. So I'm weirdly grateful for it now.

r001.rationale: He says he could work on physics simulation for fourteen hours without feeling tired because he found it beautiful, showing that enjoyment enabled extraordinary effort.

r002.rationale: He says nearly quitting revealed a mismatch between his work and values, and that he should pursue work he would do without recognition instead of forcing himself down an externally prestigious path.

astra-6.text:
It made me question whether I was pursuing something because I really cared about it or because it looked like the right next step. Getting into MIT was a milestone, but it didn’t automatically tell me what I should work on.

I think the lesson was to pay attention to the work itself: Am I curious about this problem? Do I want to keep going when progress is slow? Can I see why solving it matters? Those questions became more useful to me than whether a particular path looked prestigious.

That doesn’t mean you should quit whenever things get difficult. It means understanding whether the difficulty is part of doing something you care about, or a signal that you’re heading in the wrong direction.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes curiosity and caring about the work, but does not state that enjoying it enables him to invest extraordinary effort.

r002.rationale: It says to question whether a path is right and distinguish meaningful difficulty from heading in the wrong direction, but does not clearly say he learned to forgo work he does not enjoy instead of forcing himself to pursue it.

sol-6.1.text:
Nearly dropping out forced me to ask a more basic question: What kind of work do I actually want to do? When you’ve worked hard to get somewhere like MIT, it’s easy to assume that getting there means you’re on the right path. But you still have to figure out what matters to you.

For me, the lesson was to pay attention to the problems I felt drawn to, rather than choosing work mainly because it looked impressive. That doesn’t mean the right work is easy. It means that when it gets difficult, you still have a reason to keep going.

r001.rationale: The response says that feeling drawn to a problem gives him a reason to keep going through difficulty, but it does not state that enjoying the work enables extraordinary effort.

r002.rationale: The response advises choosing problems he feels drawn to over impressive-looking work, but does not say he should forgo work he does not enjoy rather than force himself to pursue it.
